full_judgment: 5. Controverting the submissions made by the learned Attorney-General Mr. Mahbubur Rahman placed before us the decision reported in 27 DLR (AD) 29 (Lutfun Nahar Begum vs. State) wherein the word "offence" as incorporated in section 30 of the Evidence Act has been explained and considered by the Appellate Division. It has been held that the language of the section does not render the confession of a co-accused as evidence within the definition of section 3 of the Evidence Act. It simply says that the Court may "take into consideration such confession" which only lend assurance to other evidence. He also placed before us the decision reported in 37 DLR (AD) 139 (Amir Hossain Howlader & ors vs. the State) wherein it has been held that the statement of co-accused does not fall within the definition of evidence as given in section 3 of the Evidence Act. It has been held that this is for the simple reason that it is not made on oath, that it is not made in presence of other person affected and that its veracity is not tested by cross-examination. It is, therefore, a very weak evidence against a co-accused, if it is regarded as evidence under section 30. It has also been held that the confessional statement of a co-accused is much weaker than the evidence of an approver which fulfills all the three ingredients of "evidence". Mr. Mahbubur Rahman also placed the case of Abdul Hakim and others vs. State, reported in 1987 BCR (AD) 143, wherein it has been held that for considering the prayer for bail the direct overt acts alleged against the persons named in the FIR are required to be considered. If it were found that some of the accused persons although present and named in the FIR did not take any leading and active part in the alleged assault upon the deceased which caused his death and caused no other serious offence, they are entitled to bail. It has also been held that merely because a person's name is mentioned in the FIR and charge-sheet along with others in a case under section 302 of the Penal Code does not automatically debar him from getting bail unless it is found that he is connected in some direct manner with the offence of murder. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that in view of the nature of the evidence collected by the prosecution and in view of the aforesaid decisions the petitioner may be, enlarged on bail. It has also been pointedly submitted by Mr. Rahman that in the statement recorded under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure of Major General M Khalilur Rahman it has been mentioned that the whole planning of the operation was made by this petitioner who is nothing but a housewife. He submits that for a housewife to plan such an operation is simply unbelievable and improbable.
